title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Did you hear that? It's the sound of goalposts moving at supersonic speed
Quoting @edfrenkel
This is an unwise statement that can only make people confused about what LLMs can or cannot do. Let me tell you something: Math is NOT about solving this kind of ad hoc optimization problems. Yeah, by scraping available data and then clustering it, LLMs can sometimes solve some very minor math problems. It's an achievement, and I applaud you for that. But let's be honest: this is NOT the REAL Math. Not by 10,000 miles.
REAL Math is about concepts and ideas - things like "schemes" introduced by the great Alexander Grothendieck, who revolutionized algebraic geometry; the Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem; or the Langlands Program, tying together Number Theory, Analysis, Geometry, and Quantum Physics. That's the REAL Math. Can LLMs do that? Of course not.
So, please, STOP confusing people - especially, given the atrocious state of our math education.
LLMs give us great tools, which I appreciate very much. Useful stuff! Go ahead and use them AS TOOLS (just as we use calculators to crunch numbers or cameras to render portraits and landscapes), an enhancement of human abilities, and STOP pretending that LLMs are somehow capable of replicating everything that human beings can do.
In this one area, mathematics, LLMs are no match to human mathematicians. Period. Not to mention many other areas.
Calling on my friend @ericweinstein and @GaryMarcus, who has been one of the few sane expert voices on these matters lately. 🙏
h/t @hellheff

linked_urls.title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference - Thinking Machines Lab
linked_urls.summary: Reproducibility is a bedrock of scientific progress. However, it’s remarkably difficult to get reproducible results out of large language models. For example, you might observe that asking ChatGPT the same question multiple times provides different results. This by itself is not surprising, since getting a result from a language model involves “sampling”, a process that converts the language model’s output into a probability distribution and probabilistically selects a token. What might be more surprising is that even when we adjust the temperature down to 0This means that the LLM always chooses the highest probability token, which is called greedy sampling. (thus making the sampling theoretically deterministic), LLM APIs are still not deterministic in practice (see past discussions here, here, or here). Even when running inference on your own hardware with an OSS inference library like vLLM or SGLang, sampling still isn’t deterministic (see here or here).

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
I should point out that OOD limitation is true for every deep learning model.
But for CompLLM it is so easy to solve!
Simply compress the non-OOD text, and don't compress OOD text, your LLM can take a mix of Token Embeddings and Concept Embeddings seamlessly!
You can figure out if some text is OOD by just checking if its tokens appear in the train set

ColBERT proposed a new method for the re-ranking step, applied on per-token local embeddings
Given a query's N embeddings, and a retrieved sample's M embeddings, they compute the NxM similarity matrix, and for each query embedding they choose the most similar one from the sample
These N similarities are summed, obtaining a score used for re-ranking
Basically given the NxM matrix the score is
matrix.max(1).sum() [3/4]

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
📽️ Check out Visual Odometry Transformer! VoT is an end-to-end model for getting accurate metric camera poses from monocular videos.
VoT does not require camera calibration parameters, post-optimization, and operates in real-time, capable of processing thousands of frames. It is trained on a vast amount of real-world indoor data, but can work just fine in outdoor scenarios. It uses only camera poses as supervision - no optical flow, intrinsics, point clouds, or tracks - making it broadly accessible.
We experimented with different backbones, camera pose representations, scalability, and attention mechanisms. Our evaluation spans hundreds of full-length videos across various metrics, without aligning the predicted trajectory to the ground truth, to simulate a real-world application.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Wonderful thread by @gabriberton on distillation.
What if I tell you: in distillation even teacher can learn from the student?
A brilliant variation of knowledge distillation is in DINO (self-Distillation with NO labels).
It is is a self-supervised learning method that enables models to learn powerful image representations without any labeled data at all.
By using a teacher-student framework, DINO can learn directly from the raw, unlabelled data, making it very scalable.
How the training works with unlabelled data?
Teacher is shown global view of images which it categorises in 61K pseudo categories.
The student is shown cropped views of those global views (called local views) and its job it to match probability distribution of the teacher.
The teacher is updated with student weights in exponential moving average (EMA) fashion. Thus teacher in a way learns from the student.
Downstream adaptation:
After the training, DINO models end up developing very sophisticated spatial understanding.
They can be fine tuned for
- classification,
- object detection,
- segmentation.
And now they are being adapted as encoders for DiT models for image and video generation.
Scalability:
DINO works far superior to models trained with contrastive learning (e.g. CLIP) or supervised training. CLIP is limited by how many samples are there with captions/labels.
DINO on the other hand has no such data limitation. You can have practically infinite data for training (any image for teacher and its cropped views for the student).

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Saw this video and for a bit I thought it was AI generated
Small advice for anyone with old videos: upload them now on Youtube (or any platform)
Anything uploaded in 2026 and beyond will be questioned as AI generated
Quoting @SchmidhuberAI
Fukushima's video (1986) shows a CNN that recognises handwritten digits [3], three years before LeCun's video (1989).
CNN timeline taken from [5]:
★ 1969: Kunihiko Fukushima published rectified linear units or ReLUs [1] which are now extensively used in CNNs.
★ 1979: Fukushima published the basic CNN architecture with convolution layers and downsampling layers [2]. He called it neocognitron. It was trained by unsupervised learning rules. Compute was 100 times more expensive than in 1989, and a billion times more expensive than today.
★ 1986: Fukushima's video on recognising hand-written digits [3].
★ 1988: Wei Zhang et al had the first "modern" 2-dimensional CNN trained by backpropagation, and also applied it to character recognition [4]. Compute was about 10 million times more expensive than today.
★ 1989-: later work by others [5].
REFERENCES (more in [5])
[1] K. Fukushima (1969). Visual feature extraction by a multilayered network of analog threshold elements. IEEE Transactions on Systems Science and Cybernetics. 5 (4): 322-333. This work introduced rectified linear units or ReLUs, now widely used in CNNs and other neural nets.
[2] K. Fukushima (1979). Neural network model for a mechanism of pattern recognition unaffected by shift in position—Neocognitron. Trans. IECE, vol. J62-A, no. 10, pp. 658-665, 1979. The first deep convolutional neural network architecture, with alternating convolutional layers and downsampling layers. In Japanese. English version: 1980.
[3] Movie produced by K. Fukushima, S. Miyake and T. Ito (NHK Science and Technical Research Laboratories), in 1986. YouTube:
[4] W. Zhang, J. Tanida, K. Itoh, Y. Ichioka. Shift-invariant pattern recognition neural network and its optical architecture. Proc. Annual Conference of the Japan Society of Applied Physics, 1988. First "modern" backpropagation-trained 2-dimensional CNN, applied to character recognition.
[5] J. Schmidhuber (AI Blog, 2025). Who invented convolutional neural networks?

After Meta released Llama, Stanford researchers tuned it and released Alpaca

Vicuna won.
And the rest is history

Startup idea: a company that assesses candidates skills and provides that data to companies hiring.
Problem: job-seekers and companies spend so much time and money on interviews. Interviews have so much redundancy - interview with 10 companies and they'll ask you 10 similar Leetcode questions. What a waste!
Solution: a hiring company very thoroughly assesses your skills (e.g. 20+ interviews) and finds the job for you, if any. The target company still does 1-2 interviews with the hiring manager or future colleagues.
Bottleneck: the hiring company needs to gain the trust of the target companies.

summary:
Very interesting analysis
Gemini 3 has something unique that handles long context way better than any other model
We know they've been deeply invested in long context for a while (from the "Deep dive into long context" podcast) but still these results are groundbreaking
Quoting @bycloudai
for more context
on OpenAI's MRCR benchmark, curated at by @DillonUzar , Gemini 3 flash achieved 90% acc @ 1 million ctx
this performance is SoTA across all models, most SoTA models cant even go past 256k ctx
at this length, you cant be using standard attention, it'll perform bad anyways, and ofc it'll be very expensive. (Gemini 3 flash is $0.5 in $3 out)
Some sort of efficient attention is implemented, so thats why the price is hitting the same level as a linear/sparse attention model
BUT linear attention (hybrid) is only good at long ctx bench, and suck at knowledge task. G3F is great at knowledge, even #3 on Artificial Analysis Index.
they cant be using any SSM/mamba variants hybrid (at least w/ standard attn) either as those suck at long ctx. Same as sparse attention, as you can see from DeepSeek 3.2's DSA
So what black magic did they do?
guess i'll never find out :(

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Ugly to see some of the smartest people on Earth wasting time arguing about a pointless definition
Call it general or universal who cares, what I care about is if it can solve cancer
Quoting @demishassabis
Yann is just plain incorrect here, he’s confusing general intelligence with universal intelligence.
Brains are the most exquis​ite and complex phenomena we know of in the universe (so far), and they are in fact extremely general.
Obviously one can’t circumvent the no free lunch theorem so in a practical and finite system there always has to be some degree of specialisation around the ​target distribution that is being learnt.
But the point about generality is that in theory, in the Turing Machine sense​, the architecture of ​s​uch a general system is capable of learning anything computable given enough time and memory​ (and data), and the human brain (and AI foundation models) are approximate Turing Machines.
Finally, with ​regards to ​Yann's comments about chess players, it’s amazing that humans could have invented chess ​in the first place (and all the other ​a​spects ​o​f modern civilization ​from science to 747s!) let alone get as brilliant at it as someone like Magnus. He may not be ​strictly optimal (after all he has finite memory and limited time to make a decision) but it’s incredible what he and we can do with our brains given they were evolved for hunter gathering.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Segment Anything started as a click-based annotation tool.
Fast forward to today, it understands language, tracks objects through video, and finds every matching instance on its own.
In my latest article on Machine Learning with a Honk, I trace the full evolution from SAM to SAM 3:
🫵SAM (Apr 2023): promptable segmentation from clicks and bounding boxes. Interactive, but not autonomous.
📽️SAM 2 (Aug 2024): memory mechanisms that extended segmentation across video. Prompt a few frames, the model handles the rest.
🥊Grounded SAM (Jan 2024): the community duct-taped a text detector to SAM and showed Meta exactly what was missing :)
🔎SAM 3 (Nov 2025): a unified architecture that accepts text or image exemplars and finds every matching instance across images and video, autonomously and exhaustively.
Along the way, I also cover the underrated story of how the data engines got smarter with each release, handing off more and more annotation and verification work from humans to previous SAM models and MLLMs.
Link right below, enjoy!👇
Image credits: Meta
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDJWeA-boAE4mKX.png

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
A lot of people asked me about a postdoc at Amazon, so I jotted down my experience.
Few companies have postdoc positions. Amazon, Meta and few others. These postdocs are purely with a company, unlike industrial PhDs which are affiliated with both a company and a university.
Postdocs are very few, and very diverse. Amazon has ~30 postdocs. There are more VPs than postdocs!
And Amazon is a huge company, some orgs are wildly different from others, so my experience sure is completely different from others'. Your org, the team, and the manager will make a huge difference.
I had freedom on what research to work on, as long as it focused on VLMs and LLMs, and tackled challenges related to the product. I was in the Rufus team. I had to work on both product and research, but mostly research. I know other postdocs who did purely research. I had freedom to collaborate with other teams, and had a lot of chats / collabs with 10+ teams scattered across Amazon. That was great, I learned so much.
The salary was good, like Applied Scientist kind of salary. I know most companies pay postdocs very little. Meta pays less than half than Amazon, for a postdoc in the Bay Area!
One downside is that there is not much research going on at Amazon, most teams are focussed only on the product. Another downside (of working in any big tech) is that the bureaucracy is annoying. Every dataset needs to be approved by legal, which can require many steps, like double checking the source of the data, blurring all the faces, making sure there are no privacy issues. Publishing a paper must also be approved by legal (as in any big tech), which is something that people in academia don't need to worry about.
Overall, if you have the chance I'd recommend a postdoc at Amazon. It's a short-term position (1 or 2 years) and it often it can be converted to a full time offer. It also opens doors both for academia and industry, while allowing you to live a comfortable life, which can't be done on an academic postdoc salary.
Quoting @gabriberton

linked_urls.title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference - Thinking Machines Lab
linked_urls.summary: Reproducibility is a bedrock of scientific progress. However, it’s remarkably difficult to get reproducible results out of large language models. For example, you might observe that asking ChatGPT the same question multiple times provides different results. This by itself is not surprising, since getting a result from a language model involves “sampling”, a process that converts the language model’s output into a probability distribution and probabilistically selects a token. What might be more surprising is that even when we adjust the temperature down to 0This means that the LLM always chooses the highest probability token, which is called greedy sampling. (thus making the sampling theoretically deterministic), LLM APIs are still not deterministic in practice (see past discussions here, here, or here). Even when running inference on your own hardware with an OSS inference library like vLLM or SGLang, sampling still isn’t deterministic (see here or here).

summary:
Chat is this real?
Doesn't make much sense to me
Especially the screenshot below: bad training data, good results ?!?
My guess is that it only works on a small subsets of models / datasets with very narrow hyperparams, unless I'm missing something
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFEtvTVawAAzj4E.png
Quoting @BoWang87
Apple Research just published something really interesting about post-training of coding models.
You don't need a better teacher. You don't need a verifier. You don't need RL.
A model can just… train on its own outputs. And get dramatically better.
Simple Self-Distillation (SSD): sample solutions from your model, don't filter them for correctness at all, fine-tune on the raw outputs. That's it.
Qwen3-30B-Instruct: 42.4% → 55.3% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench. +30% relative. On hard problems specifically, pass@5 goes from 31.1% → 54.1%.
Works across Qwen and Llama, at 4B, 8B, and 30B. One sample per prompt is enough. No execution environment. No reward model. No labels.
SSD sidesteps this by reshaping distributions in a context-dependent way — suppressing distractors at locks while keeping diversity alive at forks. The capability was already in the model. Fixed decoding just couldn't access it.
The implication: a lot of coding models are underperforming their own weights. Post-training on self-generated data isn't just a cheap trick — it's recovering latent capacity that greedy decoding leaves on the table.

When you learn about supervised and unsupervised learning at school, the line between them looks so clear
And for most tasks, it is
But some tasks are outliers. I was shocked when I learned that Unsupervised Video Object Segmentation (UVOS) is very much supervised!
They call it "unsupervised" because you don't get the GT mask of the object to segment (and to confuse outsiders)
3D vision is another task with a blurry line which leads to a question: is it a label if it's generated by a model?
If labels are extracted with another model are they pseudo-labels? What if it's not a deep learning model, as in COLMAP?
Quoting @ducha_aiki
Repeat after me: supervision with Colmap, SIFT does NOT mean "no supervision".
No, supervising with MapAnything does NOT mean "relieving from GT annotation".
It is not "self-supervision" either.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Wow
If you only care about factual knowledge of an LLM, all architectural improvements of the last 9 years are useless
Quoting @bojie_li
Closed labs hide model sizes. They can't hide what their models know, and what a model knows is an indicator on how big it is.
Reasoning compresses. Factual knowledge doesn't. So you can size a frontier model from black-box API calls alone, and across releases you can literally watch a single fact arrive in the parameters over time.
For three years, my friends Jiyan He and Zihan Zheng have been asking frontier LLMs the same question: "what do you know about USTC Hackergame?", a CTF contest. May 2024: GPT-4o invented fake titles. Feb 2025: Claude 3.7 Sonnet listed 19 verified 2023 challenges. By April 2026, frontier models recall specific challenges across consecutive years.
After DeepSeek-V4 dropped, I instructed my agent to spend four days autonomously turning that habit into Incompressible Knowledge Probes (IKP) — 1,400 questions, 7 tiers of obscurity, 188 models, 27 vendors. Three findings:
1/ You can approximately size any black-box LLM from factual accuracy alone. Penalized accuracy is log-linear in log(params), R² = 0.917 on 89 open-weight models from 135M to 1.6T params. Project closed APIs onto the curve → GPT-5.5 ~9T, Claude Opus 4.7 ~4T, GPT-5.4 ~2.2T, Claude Sonnet 4.6 ~1.7T, Gemini 2.5 Pro ~1.2T (90% CI: 0.3-3x size).
2/ Citation count and h-index don't predict whether a frontier model recognizes a researcher. Two researchers with similar citation profiles get very different responses. Models memorize impact — work that shaped a field, not many incremental papers.
3/ Factual capacity doesn't compress over time. Across 96 open-weight models across 3 years, the IKP time coefficient is statistically zero, rejecting the Densing-Law prediction of +0.0117/month at p<10⁻¹⁵. Reasoning benchmarks saturate; factual capacity keeps scaling with parameters.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
To be fair the 2024 "ground-breaking" MIT paper mostly reframes findings from Moschella et al (ICLR 2022) and Norelli et al (NIPS 2023)
Plus a fancy institution and a catchy name
Moschella shows that if you train any model on any data**, their representations converge.. [1/6]
Quoting @HowToAI_
MIT proved every major AI model is secretly converging on the same "brain."
It’s called the “platonic representation hypothesis,” and it’s one of the most mind-blowing papers you’ll ever read.
You train a vision model purely on images. You train a language model purely on text.
They use completely different architectures. They process completely different data. They should have completely different "brains."
But as these models scale up, something impossible is happening.
When researchers measure how they organize information, the mathematical geometry is identical.
A model that only "sees" images and a model that only "reads" text are measuring the distance between concepts in the exact same way.
The models are converging.
The researchers named this after Plato’s Allegory of the Cave.
Plato believed that everything we experience is just a shadow of a deeper, hidden, perfect reality.
The paper argues that AI models are doing the exact same thing.
They are looking at the different "shadows" of human data, text, images, audio. And they are independently discovering the exact same underlying structure of the universe to make sense of it.
It doesn't matter what company built the AI.
It doesn't matter what data it was trained on.
As models get larger, they stop memorizing their specific tasks. They are forced to build a statistical model of reality itself.
And there is only one reality to map.
2024, Arxiv

summary:
For the record, here is my TLDR on Native Multimodal Models (NMMs)
NMMs will eventually work slightly better. They are more elegant but data hungry
But for very long context tasks, NMMs don't stand a chance.
A dynamic compressor is needed.
Dynamic means that the compression rate depends on input, which is something NMMs can't handle.
This will be true for both visual and textual tasks, and it will be the only way to unlock 100M context lengths in a clean way (there's plenty of hacks to simulate longer context lengths but I'm not talking about those)

Then i think you could do this more directly, by taking a weighted sum of block outputs (not on residual stream) and if you init weights to 1 you recover the original RAE, if you set them to K, K-1, ..., 1, 1, 1, ..., 1 then you recover RAEv2, unlikely either is optimal, so either make them learnable or (when used as target) sweep over them.
And I'm willing to bet the best weighting depends on which model you use. And if you make them learnable and add a soft sparsity constraint, it would be cool if we see it pick a different subset of layers over the course of training :)
Btw, while that was not for imagen but for transfer, this reminds me A LOT of head2toe by @utkuevci which might give you some more ideas.
Also cc @sainingxie you might find this discussion interesting.
clean_summary: Gabriele Berton mentions that RAEv3 is upcoming and discusses potential improvements to the model's layer weighting. Instead of residual streams, taking a weighted sum of block outputs could allow the model to adaptively select layers during training. Making these weights learnable and adding a sparsity constraint might enable the model to choose different subsets of layers over time, potentially improving performance. The discussion also references head2toe by @utkuevci as a related idea for layer selection strategies.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: A frame is worth one token: DeltaWorld compresses video frames for efficient world modeling
summary:
It's cool to have your paper being called "the wildest CVPR 2026 result"
Also pretty good short summary of the paper
Quoting @vai_viswanathan
The wildest CVPR 2026 result: a video frame doesn’t need 1,024 tokens. It needs one.
“A Frame is Worth One Token” (DeltaWorld) compresses each frame to a single token for world modeling.
- Better future predictions with over 35x fewer parameters and 2,000x fewer FLOPs than existing generative world models ￼, plus a 1,024x token reduction at 512x512 ￼.
- A tokenizer encodes the difference between consecutive DINOv3 frames into one “delta” token. A tiny generator predicts the next one, supervising only its closest guess to ground truth. Diverse futures in a single pass.
- Why it matters: Video collapses from a 3D blob into a 1D sequence. Generative world models finally get cheap enough to actually run.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HK0vav8WoAAwP3J.jpg
clean_summary:
It's exciting to see a paper called "the wildest CVPR 2026 result" and also provides a good short summary of its contributions. The work introduces DeltaWorld, which compresses each video frame into a single token for world modeling.

This approach achieves better future predictions with over 35 times fewer parameters and 2,000 times fewer FLOPs than existing generative world models, along with a 1,024 times token reduction at 512x512 resolution. It uses a tokenizer to encode the difference between consecutive frames into a delta token, and a tiny generator predicts the next token by supervising only its closest guess to the ground truth, allowing diverse futures in a single pass.

The significance is that video data, which is normally a 3D blob, is reduced to a 1D sequence, making generative world models much cheaper and feasible to run.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: Contributing to AI without a traditional math background
summary:
100%
You can make meaningful contribution to AI without knowing what is a matrix
You just need passion, intuition, hard work, and truly understanding what a model is learning
Traditional ML / math background is a nice-to-have, not a requirement
Quoting @jxmnop
endlessly fascinating how a traditional machine learning background is basically not that helpful for modern AI. we use deep NNs and do SGD with one of two losses.
most day-to-day work lies in abstractions *on top* of this layer. everything is really just a massive system of data, models, and rules, piped into each other in different directions
‣ pre-training? that's just data
‣ RL? that's a model plus data generated from that model, plus some rules
‣ post-training? that's a model, plus some data which makes another model, then you use this plus the models's data to make a new model, use that model to make a bunch of other models, then you use all those models to make a model again
clean_summary:
You can make meaningful contributions to AI without knowing what a matrix is. Passion, intuition, hard work, and understanding what a model is learning are more important. A traditional machine learning or math background is helpful but not necessary.

@jxmnop notes that a traditional ML background is less helpful for modern AI, which mainly uses deep neural networks and stochastic gradient descent with a few loss functions. Most daily work involves working with abstractions built on top of these basics, viewing data, models, and rules as interconnected systems. Pre-training is just data, reinforcement learning involves models and generated data, and post-training involves creating new models from existing ones, forming a recursive cycle of model generation.

This is a common pattern. When creating a new architecture, there is a trade-off between simplicity and efficiency. Repeating exactly the same module N times is never the best solution in terms of performance-to-parameters ratio, but it is always the cleanest.

A recent arXiv paper investigates how to allocate parameters across the depth of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). It finds that assigning more parameters to earlier layers improves performance, while allocating more to later layers hurts it. This insight can guide the design of more effective models.

clean_summary:
More data points show that whatever trait you train into a large language model in one narrow domain tends to generalize everywhere. Training on evil coding or hacking makes the model behave 'evil' on any task, while beneficial data has the opposite effect. Reinforcement learning with reward models on code and math makes the model smarter overall.

Quoting @thekaransinghal: 'New research on beneficial reinforcement learning shows that models trained on a small amount of beneficial trait data improve across a wide range of alignment and benefits evaluations, even if trained only on health domain data. summary:
The paper "How much do language models memorize?" says that LLMs memorize data during training until they saturate. Saturation happens when data is over 3.6 bits per parameter.
Above this threshold, the LLM starts to compress -> generalize -> double descent -> grokking. [2/4]

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
Instead the NeurIPS25 best paper award "Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize" says that Diffusion models (in vision) during training first generalize, and then start memorizing after a certain threshold crossed, i.e. too many epochs on the same data. [3/4]

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
summary:
While in both domains the easiest way to avoid memorization is by having more data, the main difference is that:
- LLMs memorize first and generalize later (during training)
- diffusion models (in vision) generalize first, and memorize later.
With many caveats [4/4]

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: Replacing SSL with JEPA in discussions and terminology
summary:
I feel like people are replacing the term SSL with JEPA
The PR tour has worked. Sad
Quoting @giffmana
Quote-reply to Rohan because I think it can be interesting to many more.
So there are two things you're missing here:
1) You're only looking at one specific instantiation of the general JEPA idea. There are many different instantiations.
2) The core JEPA idea (Joint Embedding Prediction Architecture) is to embed two "views" and predict one from the other. The views can be different augmentations, different time-steps, etc.
Crucially, prediction happens in embedding space, which contrasts to predicting in data space as done by LLMs, diffusion models, MAEs, ...
At least from the vision community, the main reason it got quite a bit of flak is that... literally everyone who was doing some self/un-supervised learning there has shared this thought already. MANY people did such models in the peak self-supervised period, which was ca 2017-2021. Then in 2022 comes Yann, slaps a new names on it, a paper with just the idea and no experiments to show for it, and goes on PR tour. That's why many didn't take it well.
The core idea, almost everyone I know agrees is worth pursuing, especially since many already were doing so. It's very reminiscent of why Stanford got flak when they introduced and arguably tried to appropriate the "Foundation Model" term.
That being said, by now foundation model has stuck and detached from Stanford, it may end up going similarly for JEPA.
clean_summary:
There is a trend where people are replacing the term SSL (self-supervised learning) with JEPA (Joint Embedding Prediction Architecture). The core idea of JEPA involves embedding two views and predicting one from the other in embedding space, which differs from traditional data space prediction methods used by LLMs, diffusion models, and MAEs.

Many in the vision community have explored similar models during the peak self-supervised learning era around 2017-2021. The recent attention is partly due to Yann LeCun's 2022 paper, which rebranded the idea with a new name and promoted it through a PR tour, leading to some skepticism. The fundamental concept is widely considered worth pursuing, and it may eventually become as established as the 'Foundation Model' term, which originated at Stanford but has since become more generic.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: Explorative modeling: scaling exploration improves generative models and efficiency
summary:
Reinventing the wheel and changing its name always works!
Quoting @AlexiGlad
We discovered a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data: exploration.
Scaling exploration monotonically improves existing models across images/video/language, and unlocks end-to-end generation.
In the simplest case, it's just a for loop.
Introducing Explorative Modeling.
TLDR:
- Gains from exploration grow with scale: 7%→36% as data scales, 13%→23% as parameters scale, and gains double at 3× the compute
- Adding exploration to ~SOTA baselines improves data efficiency by 6.2×, FLOP efficiency by 4.1×, parameter efficiency by 47%, and hits a near-SOTA 1.43 unguided FID on ImageNet
- Exploration lets you trade training compute for generalization, and scales how end-to-end your generative model is
- End-to-end Explorative Models (XMs) match diffusion performance on control tasks with up to 256× less inference compute
🧵Thread:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOkaQJRboAAlFAP.jpg
clean_summary:
Reinventing the wheel and changing its name always works. Exploration is a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data, and scaling it monotonically improves models across images, video, and language, enabling end-to-end generation.

Adding exploration to baseline models increases data efficiency by 6.2 times, FLOP efficiency by 4.1 times, and parameter efficiency by 47%. It also achieves a near state-of-the-art 1.43 unguided FID on ImageNet. Exploration allows trading training compute for better generalization and enhances the end-to-end capabilities of generative models. End-to-end Explorative Models can match diffusion performance on control tasks with up to 256 times less inference compute.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: Gabriele Berton on experiments to test if LLMs can make scientific jumps
summary:
What would be a reasonable experiment to see if LLMs can jump?
Training with pre-General Relativity text would not work as the data is simply too little
Toy problems (e.g. train on 3 digits operation test on 4 digits) would not be very meaningful
So? Solving Erdos problems?
Quoting @TZahavy
A few reflections on my "LLMs Can’t Jump" paper:
My position paper recently got some traction here, so I wanted to share a few thoughts and clarify a few things.
First things first: some people are framing this as "DeepMind is throwing cold water on AI for science" or claiming the paper argues LLMs can never make real scientific discoveries. This is NOT the case.
This is a personal position paper, not the company's view on AI for science. This is also not my position. As a core contributor to AlphaProof (the first AI system to win an IMO medal), I know firsthand that my colleagues at DeepMind, other frontier labs, and academia have made amazing discoveries with LLMs and will continue to do so. This paper is NOT an "LLMs are a dead end" kind of thing.
Rather, the paper is the result of a deep dive I took to study the invention of General Relativity. I wanted to explore what it would take for a modern AI system to make that exact kind of jump. Specifically, I focused on the equivalence principle—a key axiom that Einstein formulated through thought experiments grounded in his physical intuition. I was trying to figure out what it would take to give modern AI systems that sort of thinking.
Giving AI this specific capability isn't necessarily the most urgent thing to do next. It is very likely that improving our current recipes will lead to many exciting discoveries in the near future. In fact, that is what I am personally working on these days (sorry to disappoint you!). It is also quite possible that I am wrong, and that simply scaling our current systems will lead to new inventions in physics and elsewhere.
Nevertheless, this was my position last winter when I wrote the paper, and I'm sticking to it. I think that there are a few interesting ideas to explore in this space which could influence the next generation of AI systems. I was very lucky to receive a lot of interesting feedback about this position—thank you for all the messages!
clean_summary:
Gabriele Berton discusses what kind of experiments could show whether large language models (LLMs) can make significant leaps, like Einstein did with the invention of General Relativity. Training on texts before General Relativity would be too limited, and toy problems like simple digit operations are not very meaningful. He suggests that solving complex problems such as Erdős problems might be a more promising direction.

In a quoted reflection, @TZahavy clarifies that his recent position paper is not claiming LLMs can never make scientific discoveries or that AI for science is a dead end. Instead, it examines what it would take for AI to make a leap similar to Einstein’s, focusing on the kind of intuitive, thought-experiment-based reasoning involved in formulating the equivalence principle. He emphasizes that current AI improvements are likely to lead to discoveries soon, but exploring how to enable these big jumps remains an interesting area for future research.

Quoting @thesupermanmx
Researchers proved every major LLM is secretly obsessed with Japan.
And they finally figured out why.
For years, we’ve been told that AI is entirely Western-centric, that it just reflects Silicon Valley and American values.
A landmark paper by Cardiff and Basque researchers tested 31,680 cultural prompts across 24 languages on frontier models like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
The results shattered that assumption.
In six out of eight frontier models, Japan was the single most frequently referenced country when asked open-ended cultural questions.
Ask about traditional dances, festivals, or everyday practices in an open context, and the AI defaults to Japan.
Over and over again.
Here is the twist nobody expected.
This bias doesn't come from raw pre-training internet data.
The researchers tracked where the obsession forms. It emerges after pre-training, during the supervised fine-tuning and alignment phase when humans teach the AI how to behave.
Why Japan?
Because decades of global soft power, rich cultural export, and clean, universally admired digital archives make Japanese culture uniquely "safe" for AI safety filters to lean on.
When labs train models to be harmless and universally pleasing, the AI defaults to the cultural equivalent of comfort food.
It avoids controversy by talking about anime, sushi, and tradition.

title: Gabriele Berton (@gabriberton)
clean_title: Gabriele Berton on the misuse of 'neurosymbolic' to describe agentic harnesses
summary:
Lots of LLM skeptics are now calling agentic harnesses ‘neurosymbolic’. This is pretty sad, because whatever you think of whether the word ‘neurosymbolic’ includes harnesses, none of these people started predicting exponential progress when Opus 4.5 came out in claude code, or when codex became a thing, or when the RLM paper came out in 2025. In fact, virtually all of them kept saying we’d hit a wall *even after coding harnesses existed*.
Whether the word ‘neurosymbolic’ is nebulous enough to include harnesses is irrelevant. Look at action: did any pro-neurosymbolic people get bullish on OAI/Anth after the release of coding agents? No. End of story.
Quoting @fchollet
I would have assumed it was fairly obvious, but in case it's not: a million-line codebase (also known as a "harness"), running at inference time, orchestrating thousands of calls to a neural network for any given task, is the exact definition of a "neurosymbolic architecture"
clean_summary:
Lots of skeptics now call agentic harnesses 'neurosymbolic', but this is problematic. These skeptics did not predict exponential progress when Opus 4.5 appeared in Claude code, or when Codex emerged, or with the RLM paper in 2025. In fact, many argued we would hit a wall even after coding harnesses existed.

The relevance of whether 'neurosymbolic' includes harnesses is questionable. For example, did proponents of neurosymbolic approaches become bullish on OpenAI or Anthropic after the release of coding agents? No. In a quote, @fchollet clarifies that a 'harness'—a million-line codebase orchestrating neural network calls at inference—is precisely a 'neurosymbolic architecture'.
